client: I just got my midterm grade back and it was way lower than I expected. I feel like such a failure because I've been putting so much pressure on myself to keep a 4.0, and now that's ruined. Part of me wonders if talking about this will even help - the grade is already set in stone, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really disappointed about this grade, and that makes complete sense given how much effort you've been putting in. I notice your voice sounds particularly heavy right now - would you say this is hitting harder than just disappointment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
Yeah, it is hitting harder. I worked so hard for this exam, and to see that grade just made me feel like nothing I do is ever good enough. It's not just disappointment - it's like this voice in my head keeps saying I'm a failure no matter how much I try. 

The worst part is I can't even talk to my friends about it because they all did fine. I just feel so alone with this. Like they wouldn't understand why I'm taking it this hard.
therapist: That self-critical voice sounds really painful, especially when it makes you feel isolated from others who might offer support. I'm hearing how much this grade has shaken your confidence - would you be willing to explore what "good enough" might look like without that 4.0 pressure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if I can even imagine what "good enough" would look like without aiming for perfection. Every time I try to lower my standards, I just feel like I'm making excuses for being lazy. And honestly, seeing my classmates do better than me makes me feel even more isolated, not less.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real struggle between the part of you that wants to ease up on yourself and the part that fears that might mean giving up on your goals. When you mention feeling isolated from your classmates, I wonder if you've ever considered that others might be grappling with similar pressures, even if they're not showing it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess it’s possible that others feel the same pressure, but it’s hard to believe when everyone seems so put together. I feel like I’m the only one who’s struggling to keep up, and it makes me feel even more isolated. Even if they are dealing with similar things, I don’t know how that helps me feel less alone right now.
therapist: It makes sense that seeing others appear put together would intensify your feelings of isolation. That gap between how people seem and how we feel inside can be so painful. Would you be open to exploring what might happen if you reached out to just one person you trust about how you're feeling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... the few people I do trust are always so busy with their own lives. Whenever I think about reaching out, I just imagine them being annoyed or thinking I'm being dramatic. It's like my brain comes up with a million reasons why it's a bad idea before I even try. 

And honestly, even if they did listen, they wouldn't really get it. They all seem to have their lives together in ways I just can't.
therapist: Your mind seems to be working overtime to protect you from potential rejection, coming up with all these reasons why reaching out might not work. I hear how exhausting and lonely that must feel. What do you think it would be like to test just one of those predictions, maybe with the person you feel safest with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s not that simple. Even with the person I feel safest with, I keep thinking, “What if I’m bothering them? What if they don’t really want to talk to me?” It’s like my brain just spirals, and it feels easier to just stay quiet. I don’t know if testing it will actually help or just make me feel worse.
therapist: It sounds like that fear of being a burden is really powerful, and your mind is quick to jump to those "what if" scenarios. I notice you're speaking very quickly right now - would you say there's a part of you that's afraid of slowing down enough to actually reach out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, I guess I do talk fast when I'm anxious about this. It's just...when I slow down, all those thoughts about being too needy come rushing in. Like if I actually ask for help, people will realize how much I'm struggling and pull away. 

I don't know if I can stop that thought spiral once it starts. Even now, part of me is worried I'm taking up too much of your time with this.
therapist: It sounds like slowing down makes space for those painful thoughts about being "too much," and that's understandably scary. I wonder if we could explore that fear together - what do you imagine might happen if someone did see you struggling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I'm afraid they'd confirm what I already think about myself - that I'm too needy or dramatic. If someone saw me struggling, they might pull away or get annoyed, and then I'd just feel worse for burdening them. It's easier to keep it all inside than risk that rejection.
therapist: It sounds like there's a deep fear that your struggles might push people away, and that makes complete sense given how painful rejection feels. What do you think it would be like to consider that someone might actually want to support you through this, rather than pull away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s hard to believe someone would actually want to support me when I’m like this. I feel like I’m too much for people—like my anxiety and neediness just drive them away. Even when people do try to help, I feel guilty for burdening them and end up pushing them away myself. It’s like I sabotage things before they can leave me.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in this painful cycle where your fear of being "too much" actually leads you to push people away first, almost like you're protecting yourself from potential rejection. That self-protective instinct makes so much sense, even while it leaves you feeling so alone. Would you be willing to explore what might happen if, just once, you let someone see you without immediately pulling away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it's not that simple. Every time I start feeling close to someone, this voice in my head tells me they'll eventually get tired of me. It's easier to pull away first than wait for them to do it.
therapist: That voice sounds like it's working very hard to protect you from potential hurt by convincing you to pull away first. I hear how exhausting it must be to constantly brace yourself for rejection - would you be willing to explore what it might feel like to challenge that voice, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
